column4: Zero-heat-flux core-temperature pads may carry a dynamic measurement lag that heat-conduction calorimetry has corrected since the 1920s with the Tian equation. If the offset currently attributed to physiology is instrumental, it makes a different and freely testable prediction.

(2008), "A Simple Rate Law Experiment Using a Custom-Built Isothermal Heat Conduction Calorimeter", J Chem Educ 85:112, plus its online calibration supplement; describes the correction attributed to Tian (1923). https://diverdi.colostate.edu/C431/experiments/isothermal%20microcalorimetry/references/j_chem_ed_2008_v85_p112.pdf  IMPORTANT: Tian 1923 itself was never read by anyone in the chain. This is a secondary source.
column6: ZHF core-temperature pads read offset from nasopharyngeal temperature during cardiopulmonary bypass (roughly 2.3 degC), generally attributed to physiology. Philips US11366027B2 already fits a time constant to a lagged cutaneous core-temperature heat-flow sensor and inverts an exponential to recover temperature early, citing active ZHF sensing, so the general move is NOT novel. What appears unmade is the specific ZHF-plus-Tian validation.
column7: Free, retrospective, no new data collection. Obtain paired time-synchronised ZHF and nasopharyngeal traces already held by a CPB method-comparison group and test the ramp prediction: during a linear ramp the offset should equal tau x dT/dt, scale with ramp rate, flip sign between cooling and rewarming, and decay after the ramp stops. If it does, the error is dynamic; if it does not, the physiological attribution stands. All five verifiers converged on this and explicitly advised NOT porting the Tian procedure first.
column8: Scores 5 / 5 / 4. No verifier marked it refuted, but all three are below the 6 threshold and ALL THREE flagged that the scout's own source undercuts the lead. Carried verbatim from the source ledger: 1. The identification procedure is NOT in the source. The lead says tau is identified by an electrical pulse into the internal heater; the supplement uses the electrical heater only for the calibration coefficient and prescribes a THERMAL step with no heater for tau. The portability claim rests on a step the source does not perform. 2. The source partly vindicates the physiological attribution it means to displace: "the time constant is not only an instrument dependant parameter; it is an instrument and sample dependant parameter." In ZHF the sample is the patient's scalp, whose perfusion changes during cooling, which argues for a per-patient time-varying tau. 3. Magnitude and model mismatch. The source calls the Tian correction a second-order effect worth about 5%, far smaller than the roughly 2.3 degC clinical gap. Tian describes a PASSIVE open-loop calorimeter; a ZHF pad is servo-nulled closed-loop, and a lumped first-order model is only indistinguishable from the real response below Biot number 0.1, which a thick insulating pad over perfused tissue may violate. 4. Prior art exists on the general move (Philips US11366027B2). What is left is narrow. Why this one and not two others from the same batch: a welding/additive-manufacturing lead was dropped because a verifier found Wu et al. 2019 evaluating exactly the control variable the scout claimed nobody had examined, making its headline novelty claim false as written; an apple-replant lead was dropped because all three verifiers said its headline framing was false. Found by an automated literature sweep; not refereed. A hypothesis worth one cheap check, not a finding. This is a measurement-science hypothesis for device researchers; nothing here is medical or clinical advice.
